counterexample: Take k=3, n=lcm(1,2,3)=6, and i=0. Then gpf(n+i)=gpf(6)=3<=p_{pi(3)}=3, but no prime power p^v dividing 6 is greater than 3: the available prime powers are 2 and 3.
assessment_summary: Step 0009 is false when n equals lcm(1,...,k): its fallback inequality n+i<=lcm(1,...,k) need not contradict the hypothesis n>=lcm(1,...,k), because equality is possible. Indeed, for k=3 and n=6, the theorem itself predicts two integers in [6,9] having a prime factor greater than 3, whereas only 7 does.
